clue.text: Drug supplier quick to hide damage

indicators.note: Hiding a thing means putting it out of sight inside something bigger, and that is where these letters are meant to go.

parts.note: 'pacy' is the adjective for something that moves at a fast pace
plain synonym: the damage done to a person is the harm done to them

explanation.surface: A dealer moving fast to cover up the injury they have caused.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sells you a criminal dealer concealing an injury, while the supplier wanted is the legitimate shop on the high street. 'Quick' has to become the less obvious synonym before there is room for anything inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Drug supplier' → PHARMACY: the shop licensed to dispense medicines, so it supplies drugs in the legal, medical sense rather than the criminal one.

clue.text: Papa goes over child's little difficulty

indicators.note: In a down entry, being over something means sitting higher up the column, so the piece named first ends up on top.

parts.note: Papa is the radio alphabet's word for this letter
'ickle' is nursery talk — how a small child says the word little

explanation.surface: A father bending over his small child's minor trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: Radio alphabets are a setter's standby for single letters — Papa, Oscar, Tango — and 'ickle' comes from the nursery, so both halves ask you to hear a register rather than a meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: 'difficulty' → PICKLE: to be in a pickle is idiomatic English for being in an awkward fix, so the noun means a predicament.

clue.text: Some language is magnificent, showing discrimination

indicators.note: 'Some' asks for a part of what follows rather than all of it, which is how a setter points at letters lying inside the words.

parts.note: six consecutive letters, running from inside the first word, across the whole of the second and into the third

explanation.surface: Someone praising a particular tongue as a splendid thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' is doing the work: it asks for a portion of what follows instead of describing it, and the praise in the surface keeps your eye on the meaning rather than on where one word ends and the next begins.
explanation.definitionFit: 'discrimination' is the wide category and AGEISM one variety of it, so the definition is deliberately broader than the answer.

clue.text: Force to move- it's only temporary

parts.note: to force someone into doing a thing is to make them do it
shift is the everyday verb for moving something out of the way

explanation.surface: An order to get something out of the way, just for now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force' reads as a noun in the surface — a police force, a physical force — and the wordplay needs the verb instead.
explanation.definitionFit: 'only temporary' → MAKESHIFT: a makeshift arrangement is improvised to serve until the real thing arrives, so it is temporary by design.

clue.text: Relaxed government unit will keep things fresh

definitions.note: The answer is a noun but the definition is a verb phrase: the setter names the object by the job it does rather than by a synonym, which is how shop fittings are usually described.

parts.note: 'chill' is the informal adjective for laid-back and unbothered
the committee of senior ministers that runs a British government

explanation.surface: A laid-back government department that promises to bring in new ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves hide in plain sight as politics, and they only turn into shop fittings once you stop reading 'fresh' as 'new'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'will keep things fresh' → CHILL CABINET: the refrigerated open display case in a British supermarket, whose whole purpose is keeping food cold.

clue.text: Boozers: quite attractive, some say

indicators.note: 'Say' points at speech, and the phrase tells you to trust how a word sounds in some mouths rather than how it is spelt.

parts.note: 'luscious' means richly attractive, and spoken at speed its ending flattens into a plural noise written quite differently

explanation.surface: A verdict passed on the pub regulars: fairly good-looking, if you ask around.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'luscious' quickly and the whole join appears — the compliment in the surface and the insult in the definition are the same sound.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Boozers' → LUSHES: a lush is a habitual heavy drinker, and the plural noun answers the plural noun in the clue.

clue.text: Superior but essentially stupid experts

indicators.note: 'Essentially' means at the essence, the heart of a thing, so it asks for the letters in the centre of a word and not those at its edges.

parts.note: the two letters sitting at the dead centre of this six-letter word
the three letters at the centre of this seven-letter word, in the order they stand

explanation.surface: A dismissal of some specialists as basically dim, however grand they look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Essentially' is doing positional work rather than describing anybody: the setter's sense is 'at the very heart of', which points into words instead of at them.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Superior' → UPPER: higher in position or rank — an upper floor, the upper hand — rather than better in quality.

clue.text: Criminal had a nice big property in Mexico

indicators.note: 'Criminal' describes something crooked and out of order, and letters that are out of order are letters you may rearrange.

parts.note: anagram fodder — the eight letters to be re-ordered

explanation.surface: A crook turns out to own a handsome large house in Mexico.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' reads as the noun the sentence is about, which is exactly what stops it looking like an instruction; the fodder is sitting in plain sight right after it.
explanation.definitionFit: 'big property in Mexico' → HACIENDA: the Spanish word for a large estate and its main house, used throughout Mexico and Latin America.

clue.text: Son, in better shape, that's useful around the garden

definitions.note: The definition is a relative clause describing what the object does, not a noun that could stand in its place; setters often define a tool by its job.

parts.note: the standard abbreviation for son, as used in family trees and name lists
someone trim is fit and neat, so being in better shape makes them trimmer

explanation.surface: A son who has got fitter and now earns his keep outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'Son' makes it look like someone being addressed, which hides the fact that the word is worth a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: 'that’s useful around the garden' → STRIMMER: the British name for a string trimmer, the whirling-nylon-line tool that cuts grass along edges.

clue.text: Registers offence after attack on king?

indicators.note: 'After' places the thing named before it at the back, so the offence follows the other piece instead of leading.

parts.note: in chess, an attack that puts the king in danger is announced with this one word
an offence against a moral or religious code

explanation.surface: Someone's crime is recorded in the wake of an attack on the king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King' pushes you towards royalty when the answer wants chess, and the question mark is the setter admitting that the attack named is only one particular kind.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Registers' → CHECKS IN: arriving at a hotel desk or airport counter and being entered on the list is exactly registering your arrival.

clue.text: Fight about church — it will create division

definitions.note: The answer is a noun while the definition is a clause describing its effect; the setter names the object by what it does rather than by a synonym.

indicators.note: 'About' means round the outside of, so whatever it introduces is wrapped up inside the other piece.

parts.note: to spar is to fight, especially the trial kind boxers do in training
the Church of England, shortened the way a setter always shortens it

explanation.surface: A row over the church that ends up splitting the parish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Division' is the trap: the surface offers a congregation breaking into factions, and the answer is a small piece of hardware that holds two parts apart.
explanation.definitionFit: 'it will create division' → SPACER: the washer or block put between two parts to keep a gap open, so it makes a division.

clue.text: One struggling to become free professionally?

definitions.text: One struggling to become free professionally?

parts.note: read straight, this is a prisoner or a debtor fighting their way out of a bind
the word that turns the struggle into a paid act: getting loose is the performance, not a misfortune

explanation.surface: A worker fighting to break out of some professional entanglement — a contract, perhaps, or a job.
explanation.walkthrough: Struggling to get free is a predicament for most people and a living for a very few, and the question mark warns that the whole sentence is the definition, with no wordplay hiding inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue is the definition: an ESCAPE ARTIST is the performer whose act is getting out of chains and locked boxes for a living.

clue.text: Finishes down a hundred and suffers defeat

indicators.note: 'Down' is the till-counting sense, short by a stated amount, so the amount named next is missing from what you started with.

parts.note: to close a thing is to finish it, and the six letters arrive whole before anything happens to them
the Roman numeral for a hundred, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.surface: A trader ends the day a hundred short and takes a beating.
explanation.walkthrough: Roman numerals are the setter's standing shorthand for numbers — C for a hundred, M for a thousand — and 'down' is the only word telling you this one leaves rather than joins.
explanation.definitionFit: 'suffers defeat' → LOSES: to lose is precisely to be beaten, and both are third-person singular verbs, so one swaps straight in for the other.

clue.text: Something that might cut amber seal apart

indicators.note: 'Apart' means in separate pieces, and once letters are in pieces the order they were handed over in no longer holds.

parts.note: anagram fodder — nine letters to be re-ordered

explanation.surface: A tool for prising open a seal made of amber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apart' sits at the end of the sentence where a solver expects the definition, and the vague 'Something that might cut' sits at the front where the fodder usually starts.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Something that might cut' → LASER BEAM: focused laser light is used industrially to slice metal and cloth, so it is a genuine cutter.

clue.text: Excited if data field's in excellent condition

indicators.note: 'Excited' describes something stirred up and jumping about, and letters in that state will not stay in the order they were given.

parts.note: anagram fodder — twelve letters, counting the S of the apostrophe-s

explanation.surface: Someone delighted that a database field is working perfectly.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s belongs to the fodder rather than to the grammar, and the letters only reach twelve once you count it — the sort of counting a long anagram lives on.
explanation.definitionFit: 'in excellent condition' → FIT AS A FIDDLE: the old simile takes a well-tuned violin as its picture of perfect health and repair.

clue.text: Home defeat means we're going backwards

parts.note: someone at home is in — the plainest sense of the word
a defeat is a turn of fortune against you, the noun sporting and military reports prefer

explanation.surface: A home loss in the league, and a season sliding the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home defeat' is one idea to a football fan and two separate words to the wordplay, which is where the clue gets its grip.
explanation.definitionFit: 'going backwards' → IN REVERSE: a car in reverse travels backwards, and the phrase covers any motion run the wrong way.

clue.text: Tremendous destruction

definitions.note: One sense is an adjective and the other a verbal noun, so the two definitions do not agree with each other in part of speech; the answer serves happily as both.
definitions.meaning: informal British praise: first-rate, wonderful, a word for good weather and good news
the act of breaking things up, taken as a noun

explanation.surface: A report of wreckage on an impressive scale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tremendous' is the British informal use — smashing weather, a smashing time — which sits a long way from the wreckage the other half of the clue means.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Tremendous' is the informal British 'excellent'; 'destruction' is the literal breaking of things. SMASHING covers both, one as praise and one as a plain verbal noun.

clue.text: Swamp with lots of paper about company meeting

indicators.note: 'About' means round the outside, so the piece it introduces is wrapped in the other rather than added on the end.

parts.note: a quire is twenty-four sheets of paper, a stationer's measure
the annual general meeting a company holds for its shareholders, always written as three letters

explanation.surface: An office drowning in paperwork ahead of the shareholders' annual meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swamp' reads as a verb in the surface — to be buried under paperwork — and the definition needs the noun instead, a patch of boggy ground.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Swamp' → QUAGMIRE: soft waterlogged ground you sink into, which is one kind of swamp, and the word doubles for any hopeless mess.

clue.text: They hope to conquer extremely attritional places for example
Stick, broken, reunited without it

indicators.note: Something broken has come apart into pieces, and letters in pieces can be put back in a different order.
'Without' here means lacking rather than outside — the letters it names are absent from what gets shuffled.

parts.note: the word is handed over whole first, all eight letters of it
'it' names an I and a T, and both come out, leaving six letters to shuffle

explanation.surface: A snapped stick, glued back together with one bit missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' looks like the noun the surface is built on and is really the definition, in the sense of sticking something out. The deletion has to happen before the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Stick' → ENDURE: to stick something is to put up with it — 'I can't stick him' — so the verb means to bear.

clue.text: Motor includes compiler and a recording device

indicators.note: 'Includes' says one thing contains another, so the piece named next goes inside rather than alongside.

parts.note: a motor is a car in everyday British speech
the compiler is the person who built the crossword, so the word wanted is what they call themself
the letter is taken straight off the page

explanation.surface: A car with a compiler and a recording device inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A recording device' looks like one phrase and has to be cut in two, with the 'a' doing wordplay and only the last two words defining. 'Compiler' is the setter's standard way of pointing at themself.
explanation.definitionFit: 'recording device' → CAMERA: a camera records whatever is in front of it onto film or a sensor, which is recording in the plainest sense.

clue.text: Tourist puts forecaster on spot

indicators.note: In an across entry, X 'on' Y is read as Y then X, the way the pieces would stack if the row were stood upright.

parts.note: to spot something is to sight it — to catch it with the eye
a seer foretells what is coming, the old word for a prophet

explanation.surface: A tourist putting the weather forecaster on the spot with an awkward question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on the spot' is a single idiom in the surface, and the clue needs it prised into separate pieces, one of them the ordinary verb 'spot'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Tourist' → SIGHTSEER: a sightseer is a visitor going round the sights, which is what most tourists have come to do.

clue.text: Disgrace adding AI to explosive material

indicators.note: Adding one thing to another normally just joins them, and the setter is stretching it here to mean putting one inside the other.

parts.note: the standard shorthand for trinitrotoluene, the explosive
the two letters are lifted straight off the page

explanation.surface: A scandal about putting artificial intelligence into weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters use 'AI' both ways — as the initials of artificial intelligence and as two bare letters — and here nothing at all is translated.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Disgrace' → TAINT: a taint is the mark of disgrace that clings to a name, both being nouns for a stain on a reputation.

clue.text: Institution displaying objects from both ends of Venezuela

indicators.note: 'Ends' asks for the letters standing at the two edges of a word, the first and the last, with nothing from between them.

parts.note: the opening letter of the country's name
'both' is one plus the other, and the enumeration shows that the joining word is spelt out in the middle
the closing letter of the same name

explanation.surface: A gallery showing exhibits gathered from every corner of Venezuela.
explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration (1,3,1) is doing the teaching here: it tells you the ampersand in the museum's usual shorthand has to be written out as a word.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Institution displaying objects' → the V AND A: the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, the national collection of art, design and decorative objects.

clue.text: Confess to creating two sets of papers with information technology

definitions.note: The answer is the sentence a confession consists of rather than a verb that could replace 'confess' in one; the setter defines the phrase by the act of saying it.

parts.note: papers here are identity documents, and 'two sets' asks for that pair of letters written out twice
the standard short form of information technology, as in an IT department

explanation.surface: An admission of having produced two sets of paperwork with the help of computers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Papers' means identity documents rather than newspapers, and the enumeration cuts the six letters in a completely different place from the wordplay, which is what hides the join.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Confess' → I DID IT: the phrase is the confession itself, the three words a guilty party says when admitting responsibility.

clue.text: Cook our veg in French wine

indicators.note: Cooking works ingredients into something with a new shape, which is why a setter uses it for letters that come out arranged differently.

parts.note: anagram fodder — eight letters to be re-ordered

explanation.surface: A recipe instruction: cook our vegetables in wine from France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is fodder rather than a preposition, and that is the hardest letter-pair in the clue to see, because the surface needs the word as ordinary grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: 'French wine' → VIN ROUGE: literally 'red wine' in French, the phrase an English speaker borrows for an everyday bottle of red.

clue.text: Speculate about time invitees turn up

indicators.note: 'About' means encircling, so the letter it introduces is planted inside the other word rather than tacked on the end.

parts.note: to speculate about something is to guess at it
the standard single-letter shorthand for time, as in a physics formula
surface only — it paints the invited crowd arriving and hands over no letters

explanation.surface: Wondering aloud what time the invited crowd will arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speculate about' reads as one phrase in the surface and has to be split, with 'about' switching from a preposition into an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: 'invitees' → GUESTS: guests are exactly the people who have been invited, and both are plural nouns for the same set.

clue.text: Early telegraph cables initially offering short version of this

definitions.note: The definition is the bare word 'this', pointing back at the entry itself: the clue says the letters just built are its short form, so what is wanted is the phrase they stand for.

indicators.note: 'Initially' asks for what a word starts with, so each of the words before it gives up only its opening letter.
'Short version of' runs an abbreviation backwards: the letters just made are the clipped form, and the phrase behind them at full length is what goes in the grid.

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the three words, taken in the order they come

explanation.surface: Early telegraph wires could at first send only a shortened version of a message.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds a short form and leaves you to supply the phrase behind it — the Latin that ETC has always stood for, spelt out in full.
explanation.definitionFit: 'this' → ET CETERA: the clue points at its own answer, saying ETC abbreviates it, and ET CETERA is Latin for 'and the rest'.
